topic.name: Hardware — What Is Inside a Computer?

pool.name: CS Fundamentals — Hardware Inside a Computer
pool.description: 30 explained questions on hardware, CPU, RAM, storage, motherboard, power, graphics, cooling, input/output, and component cooperation. Ten questions per difficulty; tests draw two per level.

notes.title: 1. Hardware Fundamentals
notes.summary: Understand physical components, internal and external hardware, and communication between devices.
notes.contentHtml:
Objective: explain how physical components cooperate

Hardware means the physical parts of a computer system: circuits, chips, cables, screens, keys, and drives. Software supplies instructions; hardware carries them out. A keyboard is hardware, while the text editor receiving its keystrokes is software.

Internal and external

Internal components sit inside the case, such as the processor, RAM modules, motherboard, and an internal SSD. External components include a monitor, keyboard, microphone, and USB drive. The boundary depends on the design: a laptop has an integrated keyboard and screen, and storage can be internal or external. Internal does not mean important and external does not mean optional for every task.

How parts communicate

Hardware exchanges data and control signals through connections. Motherboard circuits, buses, controllers, cables, and ports provide paths between components. A bus or other interconnect is a communication path, not a storage box. A controller helps manage a device's communication. Software, especially operating systems and drivers, coordinates access to these physical paths.

When you type a letter, the keyboard reports an event. The computer processes it and updates the document and screen. Information travels through multiple components; the keyboard does not itself edit and permanently save the document.

Think in roles

Ask four questions: What receives input? What performs processing? What holds working data or saved data? What presents output? One physical device can perform several roles. A touchscreen both displays output and senses input.

Practice safely

List three visible hardware parts and three likely internal parts. Explain one data exchange between them. Use pictures or a specification sheet; do not open a case, touch circuitry, or disconnect equipment for this lesson.

notes.title: 2. CPU — Central Processing Unit
notes.summary: Connect instructions and execution to the ALU, control unit, registers, clock speed, cores, and threads.
notes.contentHtml:
The CPU executes instructions

The Central Processing Unit executes machine instructions: small operations such as adding values, comparing them, moving data, and choosing what to do next. A program consists of instructions and associated data. The CPU does not understand a document the way a person does; software translates useful tasks into operations the hardware supports.

A simplified execution cycle

  1. Fetch: obtain an instruction from the memory system.
  2. Decode: determine which operation it requests.
  3. Execute: perform the operation, using data and storing a result as needed.

Real processors overlap and optimize many steps. This model explains the basic purpose without describing every circuit.

Parts inside a CPU

  • Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU): performs arithmetic and logical operations, such as addition and comparisons.
  • Control unit: coordinates instruction execution and signals other parts.
  • Registers: very small, fast working locations inside the CPU for values and execution state.

Registers are not substitutes for the computer's main RAM or permanent storage. CPU caches also keep frequently needed data close to the processor; for now, remember that the memory system has several layers.

Clock speed

A clock helps coordinate operations. A 3 GHz clock represents about three billion clock cycles per second, not a guarantee of three billion completed program instructions. Instructions can require different work, and processors can complete multiple operations in a cycle. Architecture, workload, memory, cooling, and software also affect speed. GHz alone cannot fairly rank unrelated processors.

Cores and threads

A core is an execution unit within a processor. Multiple cores can work on different tasks or suitable parts of a task. A software thread is an execution sequence in a program. A specification such as four cores/eight hardware threads describes support for multiple execution contexts; it does not mean eight independent physical cores. Extra cores or threads help only when software can use them and other resources are sufficient.

Explain it

For a calculator's 7 + 5 operation, describe the ALU's role, the control unit's coordinating role, and why temporary values may be held in registers.

notes.title: 3. RAM — Working Memory
notes.summary: Explain why running apps need RAM and distinguish volatile working memory from persistent storage.
notes.contentHtml:
RAM is the workspace for running programs

Random Access Memory, usually called RAM, holds instructions and data actively used by running software. Imagine storage as a filing cabinet and RAM as a worktable. You bring material to the table to work with it. This analogy describes roles, not literal paper movement: loading normally copies data rather than removing the saved file.

A browser uses RAM for its running code, page data, and other working information. Opening many tabs or a large project can increase memory demand. The operating system also needs RAM. Installing a large SSD does not give applications an equally large amount of RAM.

Volatile and non-volatile

Typical main RAM is volatile: retaining its contents requires power and, for common DRAM, regular refresh. After power is lost, its working contents normally disappear. An SSD or HDD is non-volatile: it is designed to retain saved data without continuous power. Non-volatile does not mean indestructible; failures and accidental deletion can still occur.

Unsaved edits may exist only in memory. Saving asks software to write data to persistent storage. Autosave and recovery features can sometimes preserve a version, but RAM alone does not guarantee recovery. Sleep commonly keeps memory powered; hibernation, where supported, writes state to storage. Neither is a reason to avoid saving important work.

When RAM is tight

The operating system may move some memory contents to a page file or swap area on storage. This can help handle demand, but it is generally slower than accessing RAM directly. An SSD can make swapping less slow than an HDD; it still does not become the same hardware as RAM. A system may slow down or fail to open a very demanding program if resources are insufficient.

Practice

Explain why adding RAM might help someone with many active applications, but would not directly fix a full photo-storage drive. Then explain why a saved photo can survive shutdown while an unsaved edit may not.

notes.title: 4. Storage Devices
notes.summary: Compare HDDs, SSDs, removable flash media, capacity, speed, persistence, and RAM.
notes.contentHtml:
Storage keeps saved information

Persistent storage holds operating systems, applications, documents, photos, and other saved files. Capacity is how much data fits; speed describes how quickly data can be accessed or transferred. They are different properties. A larger device is not automatically faster.

HDD versus SSD

  • Hard Disk Drive (HDD): stores data magnetically on rotating platters and uses moving read/write mechanisms. It can offer economical large capacities, but mechanical access adds delay and moving parts are sensitive to physical shocks.
  • Solid-State Drive (SSD): commonly stores data in flash memory and has no moving parts for data access. It usually provides faster random access and app loading than a typical HDD. Actual speed depends on the model, connection, workload, and other components.

Neither guarantees permanent protection. Backups matter for both. Replacing an HDD with an SSD may make startup quicker, but cannot guarantee that a CPU-heavy calculation becomes equally faster.

Other flash storage

USB flash drives and memory cards commonly use non-volatile flash memory. They make data portable and are used in cameras and other devices. Their speed and durability vary; a small USB drive is not automatically as fast as an internal SSD. Use the operating system's eject or safe-removal procedure and allow writes to finish before unplugging.

Read a capacity

GB and TB describe data quantities; one manufacturer-labelled TB is typically 1,000 GB. Operating systems may display units differently, and formatting and system files consume some space. Compare free space as well as advertised capacity. Clock frequency in GHz is not storage capacity.

Storage versus RAM

A specification of 8 GB RAM and 256 GB SSD describes two different resources: working memory and persistent file space. A saved application lives on storage; when launched, needed code and data are brought into RAM and processed. RAM contents are not automatically saved just because a disk is present.

Practice

Choose which resource matters most for each need: holding a large saved video collection, keeping many apps active, and reducing file-loading delays on an old HDD. Explain your reasoning, rather than choosing the biggest number.

notes.title: 5. Motherboard and Supporting Components
notes.summary: Understand communication paths, power, graphics, and cooling without treating any part as a complete computer.
notes.contentHtml:
The motherboard connects the system

The motherboard is the main circuit board connecting the processor, memory, storage connections, and other devices. Its circuits and interconnects carry data and control signals. Buses are communication pathways. Expansion slots can accept compatible cards, such as a graphics or network card; many laptops have fewer replaceable parts. A physical slot or port must support the intended device and standard.

Ports and connections

Ports connect peripherals, networks, displays, or power. USB, HDMI, and audio sockets serve different purposes. The connector's shape alone may not establish every supported feature or speed. Some ports carry both data and power. Never force a connector; use device documentation for compatibility.

Power supply and battery

A desktop power supply converts electrical input into regulated power used by components. A laptop uses a compatible adapter and commonly a rechargeable battery. A battery supplies energy; it is not working memory or file storage. Saved files normally do not disappear just because a healthy computer is shut down. Never open a power supply or a battery: hazardous energy can remain, and repairs require qualified help.

GPU

A Graphics Processing Unit handles graphics and other suitable parallel computations. It may be integrated with the processor or provided on a separate graphics card. Integrated graphics often shares main RAM; dedicated graphics commonly has its own video memory. Displaying a document needs far less graphics capability than a demanding 3D scene. A stronger GPU does not automatically accelerate every application.

Cooling and heat

Electronic components produce heat. Heat sinks, fans, and other cooling methods help remove it. Some low-power devices are fanless. Blocked ventilation or failed cooling can cause a system to reduce speed, shut down, or become damaged. Slowing down to manage temperature is called thermal throttling.

Keep vents clear and laptops on suitable firm surfaces. Stop using equipment with a swollen battery, burning smell, or abnormal heat and seek qualified help. This lesson requires no disassembly.

Practice

Explain why a fast CPU still needs a compatible motherboard, reliable power, and adequate cooling. Identify one limitation that buying more storage would not solve.

notes.title: 6. Input and Output Devices
notes.summary: Classify devices by the direction of information flow, including devices that do both.
notes.contentHtml:
Input enters; output leaves

Input brings data or commands into the computer. Output presents or sends results out. Classify a function by information direction, not by whether the device is inside the case or how expensive it is.

Input examples

  • A keyboard supplies key events.
  • A mouse supplies movement and button events.
  • A microphone captures sound.
  • A scanner captures a physical page as digital data.
  • Sensors measure conditions such as temperature, movement, or light.

Output examples

  • A monitor presents images and text.
  • A printer produces marks on paper.
  • Speakers present sound.
  • A haptic device produces a physical sensation such as a vibration.

Processing converts received information into a useful result. For example, a microphone captures sound, software analyzes or records it, and speakers can play it back. The microphone does not itself become an output device just because the recording is later played.

Devices with both roles

A touchscreen displays output and senses touch input. A headset can combine microphone input with headphone output. A multifunction printer can scan input and print output. A game controller can send button input and provide vibration output. Network interfaces exchange information in both directions. Describe each function rather than forcing every combined device into only one category.

A complete example

During a video call, a camera and microphone supply input. CPU and possibly GPU processing helps encode and decode media, networking transfers it, and a display and speakers present output. RAM holds active data; saving a recording uses persistent storage.

Practice

Classify a temperature sensor, speaker, scanner, and vibrating touchscreen. For the last item, explain separately how it receives touch and produces visual or tactile output. Do not grant app access to your camera or microphone just to answer the exercise.

notes.title: 7. How Hardware Works Together
notes.summary: Trace an application launch and explain why performance depends on the workload and several components.
notes.contentHtml:
Follow an application launch

  1. You click an app icon. The input device reports the action and the operating system interprets it.
  2. The OS finds the app's saved executable and supporting files on storage, checks access, and arranges execution.
  3. Needed instructions and data are loaded or made available in RAM. Systems often load parts on demand rather than copying the entire app immediately.
  4. The CPU fetches instructions through the memory system, using caches and registers to work efficiently, and executes them.
  5. The app asks system services to create a window. Graphics hardware helps produce the display output.
  6. As you type, input events update working data in memory and the screen. Saving writes the document to persistent storage.

This is a simplified model: many events overlap, and details vary by OS. The important point is that no single component performs the entire job alone.

Instructions and data

Instructions tell the CPU which operations to perform; data supplies the values those operations use. Both can be represented as bits, but their roles differ. A photo on an SSD is not automatically being processed at every moment. The program must access the required information.

Performance limits depend on the task

  • Slow storage can delay startup and file loading.
  • Too little RAM can lead to swapping when many apps run.
  • A CPU-heavy computation may be limited by processor capability and how software uses cores.
  • Complex graphics may be limited by GPU performance or graphics memory.
  • Cooling, power limits, and communication speeds can restrict otherwise capable parts.

A bottleneck is a limiting resource for a particular workload. Buying the highest number in one category does not remove every bottleneck. A slow online download may be limited by the connection or remote service rather than local RAM or storage capacity.

Practice explaining

Describe how opening a saved picture differs from editing it and saving a new version. Name the roles of input, storage, RAM, CPU, GPU, and display. Then explain why a faster SSD could improve opening time but would not automatically solve insufficient RAM for a very large editing project.

notes.title: 8. Practical Activity — Read a Computer Specification
notes.summary: Analyze a fictional device, predict workload-specific limitations, and demonstrate the completion outcome.
notes.contentHtml:
Meet StudyBox A — a fictional specification

  • Processor: four physical CPU cores, eight hardware threads, up to 3.2 GHz.
  • Memory: 8 GB RAM.
  • Storage: 256 GB SSD, with 40 GB currently free.
  • Graphics: integrated GPU using shared system memory.
  • Input/output: keyboard, mouse, microphone, monitor, speakers, and USB ports.

These numbers are for reasoning, not a buying recommendation. Up to 3.2 GHz is not a promise of constant speed. Do not open or modify a real computer for this activity.

Your tasks

  1. Identify the processor, working memory, and persistent storage. Explain each role in your own words.
  2. Describe what happens when this machine opens a text editor and saves a paragraph.
  3. Predict a likely limitation when many demanding applications run together.
  4. Decide whether an additional 60 GB local video archive fits in the stated free space.
  5. Explain why complex 3D work may be limited even though the SSD loads files quickly.
  6. Classify the microphone and speakers, then describe how replacing the monitor with a touchscreen adds another input function.

Worked reasoning

The four-core CPU executes program instructions; eight hardware threads are not eight physical cores. RAM is the 8 GB working area. The 256 GB SSD keeps saved files without continuous power, but only 40 GB is free. The 60 GB archive therefore will not fit in that free space as stated. Many active applications may strain 8 GB of RAM and cause swapping, depending on their actual demand. Integrated graphics shares resources; demanding 3D work may run into GPU or memory limits. These are evidence-based possibilities, not a claim that every task will be slow.

Adding a larger SSD could help file capacity, but does not directly add RAM, physical CPU cores, or a more capable GPU. A fast processor can still slow down if cooling is inadequate. A better upgrade choice requires identifying the workload and confirming compatibility with the device.

Completion checklist

  • I can explain the CPU, ALU, control unit, and registers by role.
  • I can distinguish RAM from storage and explain volatility.
  • I can compare an HDD, SSD, and USB flash drive.
  • I can describe motherboard connections, power, graphics, and cooling.
  • I can classify input, output, and combined devices.
  • I can trace an app launch and justify a likely bottleneck from a specification.

Completion outcome

You can explain the major components and how they cooperate without merely memorizing their names. Give your own example of a saved file becoming working data and later being saved again. The topic test draws six questions: two easy, two medium, and two hard.

questions.questionText: What does computer hardware mean?
options: Only the programs installed yesterday
The physical components of a computer system
Only files saved online
The rules for naming folders
questions.explanation: Hardware consists of physical components such as chips, keyboards, screens, and drives. Programs are software.

questions.questionText: Which component primarily executes a program's machine instructions?
options: Monitor
Battery
CPU
Speaker
questions.explanation: The Central Processing Unit executes machine instructions. Other components supply power, input, output, or storage.

questions.questionText: What is the ALU's main role?
options: Perform arithmetic and logical operations
Store all files permanently
Supply electrical power
Cool the computer case
questions.explanation: The Arithmetic Logic Unit performs operations such as addition and comparisons within the processor.

questions.questionText: What is the main role of RAM in a running computer?
options: Print documents
Keep every file forever
Replace the power supply
Hold actively used instructions and data
questions.explanation: RAM provides working memory for running programs and the operating system; it is not permanent file storage.

questions.questionText: What does volatile mean for typical main RAM?
options: It cannot hold numbers
Its contents normally disappear when power is lost
It is always external
It keeps all data without power
questions.explanation: Typical main RAM requires power to retain its working contents, unlike non-volatile saved storage.

questions.questionText: Which storage device uses rotating magnetic platters?
options: CPU register
SSD
HDD
RAM module
questions.explanation: A Hard Disk Drive stores data on rotating magnetic platters. An SSD has no moving parts for data access.

questions.questionText: What is a motherboard?
options: The main circuit board connecting computer components
A type of saved document
An online search service
A fan's power button
questions.explanation: The motherboard provides physical connections and communication paths among major components.

questions.questionText: Which component specializes in graphics processing?
options: Keyboard
Power adapter
Microphone
GPU
questions.explanation: A Graphics Processing Unit handles graphics and other suitable parallel processing tasks.

questions.questionText: Which device provides sound input to a computer?
options: Speaker
Microphone
Printer
Monitor
questions.explanation: A microphone captures sound as input; speakers produce sound as output.

questions.questionText: Which device performs both input and output functions?
options: A basic speaker without a microphone
A basic keyboard without a display
A touchscreen
A basic printer without a scanner
questions.explanation: A touchscreen displays output and senses touches as input.

questions.questionText: A specification lists 8 GB RAM and 512 GB SSD. What do these describe?
options: Working memory and persistent storage, respectively
Two different CPU clock speeds
Two screen resolutions
Two identical types of volatile memory
questions.explanation: RAM holds active working data; the SSD stores saved information persistently. The capacities refer to different resources.

questions.questionText: Which CPU part coordinates instruction execution rather than primarily performing arithmetic?
options: Monitor cable
Storage platter
Battery cell
Control unit
questions.explanation: The control unit coordinates instruction execution and signals other parts. Arithmetic and logic are associated with the ALU.

questions.questionText: How do CPU registers differ from an SSD?
options: Registers are removable backup drives
Registers are small, fast working locations inside the CPU; an SSD is persistent storage
Registers store all photos without power
An SSD is the CPU's control unit
questions.explanation: Registers hold small amounts of immediate execution state or data inside the CPU, unlike a persistent file-storage device.

questions.questionText: A CPU is described as four cores and eight hardware threads. Which conclusion is justified?
options: It has eight independent physical cores
Every app will run exactly eight times faster
It has four physical cores supporting multiple execution contexts
It requires eight separate operating systems
questions.explanation: Hardware thread support is not a count of physical cores. Benefits depend on workload and available resources.

questions.questionText: Why does changing from a typical HDD to an SSD often make application loading faster?
options: The SSD usually accesses needed files with less delay
It always doubles the CPU's physical cores
It turns every saved file into RAM
It removes the need for software
questions.explanation: SSDs generally offer lower access delays and faster file operations than typical HDDs, although actual performance varies.

questions.questionText: What is a motherboard bus or interconnect used for?
options: Making the screen physically larger
Permanently storing every password
Cooling the battery with air
Carrying data and control signals between components
questions.explanation: Buses and interconnects provide communication paths, rather than acting as persistent file stores or cooling devices.

questions.questionText: A laptop slows down when its ventilation openings are blocked. What is a plausible explanation?
options: Its SSD automatically became an HDD
Heat causes the system to reduce speed to manage temperature
Its files changed from software into hardware
Its RAM capacity doubled
questions.explanation: Thermal throttling reduces performance to manage excessive temperature. Vents should be kept clear without disassembling the machine.

questions.questionText: Which sequence best summarizes opening a saved application?
options: The monitor writes instructions directly into the battery
The keyboard permanently stores the entire program
The OS arranges access to saved code, needed parts become available in RAM, and the CPU executes instructions
The SSD becomes the application's screen
questions.explanation: Launching coordinates input, OS services, storage, memory, CPU execution, and output. Loading can happen incrementally.

questions.questionText: A headset includes a microphone and headphones. How should its functions be classified?
options: Microphone input and headphone output
Only storage
Only output because both are worn on the head
Only processing
questions.explanation: The microphone captures audio input; the headphones produce audio output. One physical product can combine roles.

questions.questionText: What is the difference between storage capacity and storage speed?
options: They are both CPU clock measurements
Capacity tells the screen's size; speed tells its color
A higher capacity guarantees faster access
Capacity describes how much data fits; speed describes how quickly it is accessed or transferred
questions.explanation: Capacity and performance are distinct. Device model, interface, and workload affect speed independently of the amount of space.

questions.questionText: A computer has a large SSD, but it slows down when many memory-heavy apps are open and swap activity rises. Which change most directly addresses the indicated limit?
options: Buy a larger monitor
Add compatible RAM if the system supports it
Rename the SSD
Increase speaker volume
questions.explanation: The evidence suggests working-memory pressure. More compatible RAM may reduce swapping; more SSD capacity alone is not more RAM.

questions.questionText: A file was saved, then edited without saving again. Power fails and there is no autosave or recovery copy. What should the learner expect after restart?
options: RAM will always restore the final edits
The CPU registers permanently store the entire document
The last saved version may remain on storage, but the unsaved RAM-only edits are normally lost
Every saved file must disappear
questions.explanation: Persistent storage retains the saved version, while volatile working memory normally loses unsaved data without power.

questions.questionText: Processor A has a higher GHz rating than Processor B. Which additional information is needed before claiming A will run a particular app faster?
options: Architecture, workload, usable cores, memory behavior, and operating power or thermal limits
Only the color of the case
Only the number of keyboard keys
Nothing: GHz alone guarantees application speed
questions.explanation: Clock cycles are not a universal measure of completed work. Architecture, parallelism, memory, and thermal conditions affect application performance.

questions.questionText: StudyBox has a 256 GB SSD with 40 GB free. A learner wants to add a 60 GB local archive without removing anything. Which reasoning is correct?
options: It fits because 256 is greater than 60 regardless of used space
The 8 GB of RAM supplies the missing disk capacity
A higher CPU clock creates more free space
It does not fit in the stated free space; additional suitable storage or an approved space-management plan is needed
questions.explanation: Available capacity, not total advertised capacity, determines whether the additional archive fits. RAM and CPU frequency do not add SSD space.

questions.questionText: An SSD loads a 3D project quickly, but the scene renders slowly and the GPU is heavily utilized. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The keyboard must be too small
Graphics processing may be the workload's bottleneck; more SSD capacity alone may not improve rendering
All SSDs are volatile
The monitor is executing the program instead of the CPU
questions.explanation: Different stages can have different bottlenecks. Fast file loading does not establish that graphics computation will also be fast.

questions.questionText: Which explanation best traces typing and saving a sentence?
options: The keyboard writes directly to the SSD with no software involved
The screen is the only component involved because it shows the sentence
Input events update program data in RAM through software and CPU work; saving writes the document to persistent storage
The battery remembers each letter permanently
questions.explanation: Typing, displaying, and saving involve cooperating components. Working memory and persistent file storage have different roles.

questions.questionText: A single-threaded task runs on an eight-core processor. Why might it not become eight times faster than on a comparable single core?
options: The task cannot automatically divide its execution across all cores, and other limits may remain
Multiple cores stop all instructions from executing
Eight cores always mean eight SSDs
Only storage capacity determines computation speed
questions.explanation: Parallel speedup requires suitable software and workloads. Extra cores do not automatically parallelize one execution sequence.

questions.questionText: A learner claims that adding a USB flash drive makes 4 GB of RAM into 68 GB of RAM. What is the best correction?
options: All USB drives are CPU registers
Every flash drive is volatile main memory
USB storage cannot retain files without power
The drive adds persistent storage; any OS use of storage for paging is not equivalent to adding physical RAM
questions.explanation: Storage and RAM differ in role and access behavior. Some systems use storage to support memory management, but this does not create equivalent main RAM.

questions.questionText: A computer has powerful components but slows down after sustained work and reports high temperature. What should be investigated before assuming the CPU needs replacement?
options: Whether the text editor's font is blue
Cooling, ventilation, and thermal or power limits, using safe checks and qualified help where needed
Whether folders use uppercase names
Whether the mouse has a longer cable
questions.explanation: Sustained heat can trigger throttling even in a powerful system. Performance diagnosis should consider cooling and power rather than only component ratings.

questions.questionText: A smart control panel senses touch, reads temperature, and vibrates when an action completes. Which classification is correct?
options: Temperature sensing is output and vibration is input
Every function is persistent storage
Touch and temperature sensing are input; vibration is output, and a display also provides output
Touch is only output because the user sees the panel
questions.explanation: Classify by direction: sensors bring information into the system, while displays and haptics present results outward. A combined device can do both.
